newsitem.title: USA: Senate leader Lott wants order, not revolution.
newsitem.headline: Senate leader Lott wants order, not revolution.

text.p: Smooth-talking, deal-making Senate Majority Leader Trent Lott has emerged as the capital's most influential Republican and his party's success in the next two years hinges in large part on his political skills.

Re-elected to his party post without opposition Tuesday, the Mississippi Republican has said his goal is regular order, an ambitious objective in the notoriously sluggish Senate where any one lawmaker can stall the entire process.

Eschewing the tough talk that marked the 1994 Republican takeover of Congress -- and scared some voters -- Lott, 55, has made it clear he wants results, not "revolution." He was instrumental in reaching agreements with the White House this year on health care, immigration and other measures that played well with the public and helped Republicans keep control of Congress.

At a news conference after his re-election Lott said he wanted to keep working with President Clinton and other Democrats. "We're going to work across the aisle in an open and fair way with our Democratic colleagues for the best interests of our country," he said.

He has left no doubt, however, that he will challenge Democrats when it serves his interests. Republicans plan hearings on Democratic fundraising irregularities and Lott has challenged Clinton to make the first move on Medicare reform.

With House Speaker Newt Gingrich staggering under ethics charges and dismal public approval ratings, Lott is likely to emerge as the Republicans' chief spokesman and strategist. But he rejected suggestions he will become the party point-person, saying, "I'm not attracted to the idea that we'll have a sole leader ... I just don't work that way."

An impeccably groomed man who never has a hair out of place or a wrinkle in his suit, Lott looks like a caricature of a country-club Republican. In fact he grew up in modest circumstances in Mississippi where his father was a shipyard worker and a farmer.

Lott is a former University of Mississippi cheerleader whose demeanor is a mix of sunny buoyancy and steely determination. Unlike his predecessor Bob Dole, he has an open leadership style and consults a wide range of senators.
A solid conservative, Lott's inclusive style has earned him the support of moderates in his own party. He has also shown he has the ability to work across party lines.

"(Lott is) more inclusive. You've seen the confrontational route and to some of us that was frustrating. We want to see productive work done," said Oklahoma Republican Don Nickles, who also was re-elected Tuesday as Lott's No. 2.
But Republicans' success in the November elections -- they picked up two Senate seats, expanding their majority to 55-45 -- could complicate any quest for consensus.

Several moderate Republicans retired and the new crop of senators elected to replace them is more conservative and possibly less inclined to compromise. Democrats also plan to continue using the filibuster to increase their leverage.

Lott began as a Democratic staffer for a congressman, changing parties in 1972 when he ran for Congress. He won and served in the House from 1973 to 1989. As deputy Republican leader there, he was the intermediary between hard-charging younger Republicans like Gingrich, whom Lott described as a "back bench bomb thrower," and senior party leaders more inclined to compromise with majority Democrats.

Over the years Lott has protected federal spending vital to his state and looked out for timber and textile interests. He was known as a staunch supporter of the supply-side economics espoused by President Ronald Reagan and helped persuade conservative Democrats to vote for Reagan's first, dramatic budget plan.
He was the youngest member of the House Judiciary Committee in 1974, loyally defending then-President Richard Nixon, when it passed articles of impeachment on Watergate.

Lott moved to the Senate in 1989 and by one vote won the job of deputy majority leader under Dole in 1995. He was elected to the top post when Dole retired from the Senate last June to give full time to his presidential campaign.
He was born Oct. 9, 1941, graduated from the University of Mississippi Law School and studied international law at the University of Dublin. He and wife Patricia have two children.
